newsitem.title: USA: Greek economy minister sees '97 growth at 3.5 pct.
newsitem.headline: Greek economy minister sees '97 growth at 3.5 pct.

text.p: Private and public investment, coupled with falling inflation and declining interest rates, will allow Greece's economy to grow at a rate of 3.5 percent in 1997, the country's economy minister said.

Speaking to a meeting sponsored by the Harvard Business Club, Yannos Papantoniou, minister of the economy and finance of Greece said: "Growth is expected to reach 3.5 percent. It is sustaned by both private and public investments."
In addition, he said inflation, which is running around six percent, should end the year at around five percent.

Papantoniou said the "the major force" that has led the country's recovery and has helped Greece to achieve economic stabilization with growth has been the drop in inflation over the past three years and falling real interest rates.
He also said the fiscal deficit is expected to fall to 4.2 percent of the country's gross domestic product (GDP) this year, which would be a decline of about 10 percentage points from 1992 levels.
"That is perhaps the largest budget savings achieved in Europe for this period," the economy minister noted.

Papantoniou said the current trends should also allow Greece to achieve the economic milestones set out in the Maastricht Treaty by 1998 or early 1999 and will thereby allow the country to participate in the European Monetary Union (EMU) by 2000 or 2001.
Turning to the labor market, Popantoniou said discussions about reforming the labor market will start in April or May.

On the privatization front, the economy minister said the government is open to selling off certain state-run industries but social sectors such as health and education would remain in the hands of government.
"We hope by the end of this decade, the macroeconomic and micoreconimc adjustment will be completed," he added.

Looking to the region as a whole, Papantoniou said the Greek government will entertain an initiative to propose to the U.S. government, the Europen Union and to major financial instutitions such as the World Bank and European Bank for Reconstruction and Development to put together a new program for the consstruction and development of the Southern Balkans and the Black Sea area.
"These governments need assistance. Self help won't do," he said, noting that by helping them, economic and political issues would be resolved over the medium and long term.
